content.title: Not good enough object detection submission
content.review:
-This paper proposes a Mixture Density Object Detector (MDOD), which models the detection as a problem of density estimation. It claims to avoid the ground truths assignments (GTA) which is commonly used in almost all object detection works.  However, in the section of "RoI sampling", it clearly says that the proposed method still needs a threshold for roi sampling. This is no much different from the standard GTA, which is contradictory with the claim of this paper.

-The idea of modeling detection as density estimation is OK, but not very interesting to me.

-The results are OK, but not surprising good, especially when the baselines are kind of low. Please check the baseline of Detectron2, and the recent state-of-the-art detection results.

A few questions:

-Don't quite understand why the "mixture model" is across all spatial locations (\pi summed over all locations equal to 1). There could be multiple objects presented in one image.  If \pi summed over all locations equal to 1, the presence of an object will suppress the presence of the other object? And the value of \pi at a location will be very small.

-Why no class loss for ground truths bounding boxes in L_{MoC}?

-The proposed method doesn't guarantee the +/- balance. You already did roi sampling, why not control the ratio explicitly?
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: The answers to your opinions
content.comment:
Thank you for the efforts and valuable feedback in reviewing our paper.

---
**[RoI sampling, GTA]**
Our method separates localization and classification loss as shown in Eq. (4) and (5). For localization, the network is trained so as to maximize the likelihood of GT boxes. Therefore, we do not use any GTA nor a comparison of RoIs with GTs. For classification, RoI sampling is performed. To obtain the bounding boxes including background classes, we sample RoIs from the estimated mixture model and if the IoU between the RoI and a GT exceeds a threshold it is trained as the class of GT. (RoI sampling) On the other hand, GTA is performed in both localization and classification, in the GTA-based method.

In the previous object detection works, the GTA means the process of directly assigning **the GTs to specific locations of the network’s output**. But, RoI sampling compares **GTs and sampled RoIs**.  According to this object detection literature, we think RoI sampling cannot be considered the same as GTA and should be differentiated. In GTA, the GT is compared directly to the output of the network, whereas in RoI sampling, the GT is compared to the sampled RoI. This difference is important because RoI sampling does not cause the heuristics, complex process, and problems mentioned in our paper (matching strategy, anchor and fg-bg imbalance). Unlike the GTA, RoIs are sampled from an estimated mixture model and are completely separate from the network structure.

In the next revision, we will revise the paper more clearly to reflect your feedback and our responses to avoid confusion about the meaning of ground truth assignment (GTA) and RoI sampling.

---
**[The idea of modeling ...]**
I think your feedback is too vague and abstract, could you explain in more detail about why it’s not very interesting to you and how we can improve about it?

---
**[The results are OK. ...]**
In our paper, performance improvement is an additive effect. The primary goal of our paper is to propose a method to train the object detector without GTA that causes heuristics and complex processing in the training of the detector. We successfully train the detector without GTA through density estimation using a mixture model and showed higher AP compared to EfficientDet (one of the SOTA detectors) and others using the same input size. To compare the detection performance, we should consider the experimental setting rather than just comparing the AP of the table Detectron2 itself.

---
**[Question: $\pi$]**
If we use the mixture models more than one, we eventually have to assign a ground truth box to a specific mixture model. Because only one mixture model is used in our method, we can train an object detection network without ground truth assignment.

For training based on density estimation using the mixture model, the size of $\pi_{k}$ is not important.  The weight of the gradient for a mixture component is determined by ${\pi_{k} \times F_{k}(b_{i})} \over {\Sigma \pi_{k} \times F_{k}(b_{i})}$. Therefore, theoretically, a small value of pi does not negatively affect the training. Please refer to the training part of the Mixture Density Network (derivatives with respect to the mixture parameters).

Also in the inference phase, as mentioned in our paper, $\pi_{k}$ is normalized by the maximum value of $\pi$ for thresholding the mixture components, hence a small value of pi does not cause a problem.

---
**[Question: $L_{MoC}$]**
As explained in the paper, the GT box does not have a background box in general. $\L_{MoC}$ focuses only on localization. As mentioned in the paper, class probability is trained through $\L_{MM}$. Learning the class probability twice with GT and RoI harms the statistical meaning of class 'probability'.

For locations with a high likelihood of the estimated mixture model, the class information is learned by RoI, on the other hand, for locations with low density, the bounding box is not predicted.

---
**[Question: positive/negative balance]**
As mentioned earlier, the primary goal of our paper is to propose a method to train the object detector without GTA that causes heuristics and complex processing during the training of the detector. Controlling the ratio belongs to these heuristics and increases dependence on hyper-parameters.

---
In this paper, we propose novel ideas that were not suggested in the past to approach the object detection task from different perspective. Therefore, our work has a large room for improvements that can be achieved by further research and development. In research, we believe that it's more meaningful to explore possibilities through new ideas than to create good benchmarks. We politely ask you to consider this in the final decision.

content.title: Comments for MDOD
content.review:
This paper proposes the Mixture Density Object Detector (MDOD) that claims it can train object detectors without ground truth assignment. They formulate the object detection problem as a probabilistic density estimation problem. Experiments are conducted on MS COCO to prove the effectiveness of the method. 

They use FPN to extract multi-level features from the input image, and predict density maps with different convolutions. There are four prediction maps, for center offsets, scales, object classification, and overall constraint respectively. 

Strengthens:
This paper formulates object detection into a density estimation problem and makes their efforts for totally end-to-end object detection frameworks. 

Weaknesses:
1. My first concern for this paper is I do not think this paper is doing object detection without ground truth assignment. 
Because there is still a RoI sampling procedure in this paper, and define positive / negative samplers with corresponding IoUs with GTs. I think the main claim in this paper is incorrect or at least not precise. 

2. The experimental part cannot support the effectiveness of the method. 
I think one crucial experiment for making the work publishable is to prove the method indeed outperforms GTA-based methods. We should not do no-GTA just because of the simple of no-GTA methods. We should do no-GTA because it indeed works. 
As the authors stated in the related works, the anchor design is heuristic and complicated. But it works, and pushes forward the performance of object detection. While researchers recently find that the anchors are not necessary, because they obtain **better results** without multiple anchors. 
It is the same for this paper. The authors should prove that we can obtain better results vs. ATSS [SOTAs in GTA] with the simpler framework. 

3. The experimental part of this is not satisfactory, especially the comparisional part. 
I think the authors should directly compare the method with recent SOTA methods stated in their related work. For example, Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, FCOS, and ATSS. In my understanding, the only difference between this paper and related works are the objective functions. Because the feature extraction part is almost the same except for the number of output channels for different purposes. Current comparisons studies can not address my concerns. The results in Table 5 are unfair.
The only public detector compared in this paper is EfficientDet, because the authors are using the aggressive long-time training and data augmentations. The method outperform EfficientDet by 0.9 points with Efficient-D1. I recommend the authors compare their efficiency with EfficientDet as the paper has no strengths on performance. 

4. More analysis with keypoint-based methods are required. 
For example, CornerNet and CenterNet. Because they are also using density estimation for classification.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Weakness 4
content.comment:
**[Weakness 4]**
Performance comparison with keypoint-based methods was performed on Fig. 7 and Tab. 5. The term density estimation in our paper refers to probability density estimation, keypoint-based methods such as CornerNet and CenterNet are not based on probability density estimation. The keypoint-based methods may be seen as visualizing the density as the heatmap in a broad sense, but it does not express the probability density. Indeed, we could not find any word ‘density’ or ‘probability’ in both papers. Both MDOD and keypoint-based method are anchor free methods, but their structural characteristics, learning methods, and prediction forms are completely different from ours. It would be very kind of you, if you could explain in more detail about which analysis is more needed in comparison with keypoint-based methods.


----------
In this paper, we propose novel ideas that were not suggested in the past to approach the object detection task from different perspective. Therefore, our work has a large room for improvements that can be achieved by further research and development. In research, we think it's more meaningful to explore possibilities through new ideas than to create good benchmarks. We politely ask you to consider this in the final decision.

content.title: Weakness 1, 2, 3
content.comment:
Thank you for the efforts and valuable feedback in reviewing our paper.


----------
**[Weakness 1]** 
Our method separates localization and classification loss as shown in Eq. (4) and (5). For localization, the network is trained so as to maximize the likelihood of GT boxes. Therefore, we do not use any GTA nor a comparison of RoIs with GTs. For classification, RoI sampling is performed. To obtain the bounding boxes including background classes, we sample RoIs from the estimated mixture model and if the IoU between the RoI and a GT exceeds a threshold it is trained as the class of GT. (RoI sampling) On the other hand, GTA is performed in both localization and classification, in the GTA-based method.

In the previous object detection works, the GTA means the process of directly assigning **the GTs to specific locations of the network’s output**. But, RoI sampling compares **GTs and sampled RoIs**.  According to this object detection literature, we think RoI sampling cannot be considered the same as GTA and should be differentiated. In GTA, the GT is compared directly to the output of the network, whereas in RoI sampling, the GT is compared to the sampled RoI. This difference is important because RoI sampling does not cause the heuristics, complex process, and problems mentioned in our paper (matching strategy, anchor and fg-bg imbalance). Unlike the GTA, RoIs are sampled from an estimated mixture model and are completely separate from the network structure.

In the next revision, we will revise the paper more clearly to reflect your feedback and our responses to avoid confusion about the meaning of ground truth assignment (GTA) and RoI sampling.


----------
**[Weakness 2]** 
The most important effect of our method is that we can actually learn object detectors without GTA, GTA makes the training of a multi-object detection network too heuristic and complicated. Here, our method shows improved performance compared to the method using standard GTA. As can be seen in Tab. 3, Tab. 5, and Fig. 7, the proposed method indeed works. In recent work (ATTS), the anchors are no longer essential, but its process makes GTA-based training more complicated, instead.

GTA-based method achieved a lot of progress since deep learning was applied to object detection. ATSS is the SOTA research in this progress. Our proposed method is the first study to propose a method that trains a detector without direct GTA to the network output but via density estimation. Therefore, we think that the comparison with the standard GTA method is more appropriate than the comparison with the SOTA-GTA-based method.

According to the results of open repository that implements ATTS with EfficientDet, when using the same image size and feature extractor (backbone, and fpn), our MDOD shows better performance than ATSS on the MS COCO validation dataset.

EffcientDet-D0: 33.5 / ATSS + EffcientDet-D0: 33.8 / MDOD + EffcientDet-D0: 35.2


----------
**[Weakness 3]**
It is not true that the public detector compared in this paper is only one (EfficientDet). In Tab. 5 and Fig. 7, MDOD is compared to many other detectors. In most object detection papers, experiments are performed using only one of the '512x512 (+320x320, ...)' and 'short-800' inputs. We use the '512x512 (+320x320, ...)' as input size for our experiments. Therefore, in Tab. 5, It is difficult to directly compare MDOD with the other methods using 'short-800' input. To compensate for this, we plan to show the ‘short-800’ MDOD result that can be compared with the ‘short-800’ results of RetinaNet, FCOS, and ATSS from Tab. 5. In the next revision, we will revise the paper to reflect this experiment results.

EfficientDet is one of the SOTA object detectors using standard-GTA. MDOD with EfficientDet shows higher AP than EfficientDet. This improvement of our work is not caused by structural changes. We show that MDOD can take advantage of good structural studies through comparison with EfficientDet

We cannot agree that our MDOD is performing aggressive augmentation. Our augmentation strategy is one of the most commonly used methods. RetinaNet, FCOS, and ATSS use different augmentation strategies compared to ours. According to ATSS, they train networks using variable aspect ratio, and multi-scale training methods. These are the augmentation methods that we don't perform in our training.

Moreover, it would be nice of you to explain in more detail why the results in Tab 5 are unfair, so that we could reform our results.

display_title: a novel reformulation of object detection as a problem of density estimation of bounding box across multiple-scale output predictions

content.title: a novel reformulation of object detection as a problem of density estimation of bounding box across multiple-scale output predictions
content.review:
The paper proposes a novel approach that reformulates the object detection task as a problem of density estimation of bounding box across multiple-scale output predictions. Through density estimation, a detection network can be trained without too much heuristics caused by ground truth assignment. 

There is a list of noteworthy contributions:

1) The paper formulates the object detection task as a density estimation problem of a mixture model defined on the multi-scale predictions. The authors also propose a novel network architecture, Mixture Density Object Detector (MDOD) together with a new objective function for this formulation, which is proved to be elegant & effective.

2) As a dense detector, the label assignment process is simple, and the training is done without too much heuristics. It seems that only three hyper-parameters (i.e., N_{roi}, IOU threshold 0.5 & loss weight \alpha) are directly related to the training process.

3) The foreground-background imbalance problem in the dense detector is solved naturally as the training progresses, and there no hyper-parameter directly involved.

4) The proposed method is superior to some SOTA detectors in both AP and FPS.


In my opinion, the proposed model tries to learn everything a dense detector needed during the training process, so it might be suffering from the following problems:

1) It seems that the proposed model takes longer training time. The paper does not show the results of the  1x schedule (12 epoch), which is long enough for most dense detectors. Nevertheless, the fully converged MDOD is still competitive under fair comparison with other alternatives.

2) The paper does not show the results when input resolution becomes higher (e.g., short-800). I think this is because higher resolution input causes the K being much larger which makes the model hard to optimize.

The paper well written, and the motivation of using density estimation as a natural solution to avoid too much heuristics caused by ground truth assignment is clearly described. Overall, I think this work is worthy of acceptance and should encourage more investigation into the new framework of object detectors in the community.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Training time, High resolution
content.comment:
Thank you for the positive feedback and for highlighting the contributions of our work.

---
**[Training time]**
Compared with Faster RCNN and FCOS using the 'short-800' setting, the training time of our method is long. However, the comparison with the detectors trained in a similar setting ('320x320' and '512x512') to ours is as follows:

M2Det: 150 epoch, PASSD: 120 epoch, RefineDet: ~80 epoch  
EfficientDet: 300 epoch (from the default configuration file of EfficientDet’s official repository)  
MDOD: 160 epoch

As can be seen above, our method tends to use a long training time, but EfficientDet has much longer training time even compared to ours, so we think MDOD's training time is not a big problem.

---
**[High resolution]**
In a recent experiment of MDOD using Efficient-D2 as a backbone with 768x768 sized input on MS COCO validation set, we obtained an AP that is 0.3%p higher than the original EfficientDet-D2. However, it is also possible that the problem you mentioned may occur with larger images. We plan to show the result of MDOD using large size input (e.g. ‘short-800’). In the next revision, we will revise the paper to reflect these experiment results.
